items.title: 68356_Howard R. Scott oral history interview
items.q: some musicians didn't care for Cab because he wasn't a musician.

ctx.x: think? Well, I tell you, in those days, there weren't many colored people in Harlem. And there -- a good deal of white people came there, and you had a mixed orchestra, a couple of white women was in there. And they didn't think anything, everything was all right. We didn't have any crime in those days. We fellows used to get off from work around 3:00 or something like that, we'd go by the Amsterdam or we'd go to the Rhythm Club. Because if you're working downtown, -- now, here's something.

You're working downtown, like Roseland, we got off at 1:00. We'd come up here and the Cotton Club, and don't forget Small's Paradise. Their late show was 2:00. We got in town in time to go to those shows. Well, I didn't go to the Cotton Club because, you see, some musicians didn't care for Cab because he wasn't a musician. And he took over the other fellow's job, what was his name, had the band. They just put him up on front of this band, and he was no musician.

So I had to go where the old ones went. I followed them. Come on, Scottie, you going? I say, where are you going? Well, never mind, come on, you're with me. Go this place and that place. So after we got out, anytime it'd be daylight, we'd get out of those places. And fellows have money, never nobody hold you up or nothing like that.
